HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Thanks Good question. I'm a big fan of correlating pairs. I think it serves as a good indicator. First is to realize how one pair correlates to another. Then you watch the levels like you would any other trade. For example, this past Friday, on the GU & EU moved closed together. Watch when one pair reacted at a level then other followed. Also look at the crosses for a good indication. The EURGBP was a good indictor on Friday. AU and NU was also an easier pair to correlate. There's a benefit to trading the pair that slightly lags, just make sure you're trading the levels according to that pair. Meaning that, let's say, demand was 50 pips away on the leading pair and only 25 pips away on the lagging pair, target the 25 pips if trading the lagging pair not the 50 pips as indicated on the leading pair. Hope that helps. The following user(s) said Thank You: Ifmyante, Marek, kkb, roshan, Kadox, omidfxt For greater success figure out where the BS is and avoid it. We're certainly safest trading from the extremes of either. Just look at when price breaks an high or low, with an FTR; see the rejection which so very often occurs from the new FL on return. when this FL eventually breaks, price has entered the pole. Some may trade this break, but they must be ready to suffer DD right back through the flag, and sometimes even slightly beyond. Hence, for safety, it's usually best to let price break and form an FTR which we can trade from on return. The tg is usually the base of the pole, but if price starts showing signs of compression through the pole, watch out for possible support/resistance flips along the way, especially if price hadn't hit its target before the flag broke back into the pole. There are very many variables in this scenario, so to draw a set of charts for it would mean explaining every single PA setup there is. So I urge you to look through your charts and try to make sense of these words. Some may trade this break, but they must be ready to suffer DD right back through the flag, and sometimes even slightly beyond. You find out painfully quick with S and D levels if they are wrong (especially when there is a strong trend) - even if they tick every box on what a good level is supposed to look like. I am still finding PAZ very subjective and I have seen many seemingly good levels engulfed that make absolutely no difference to where price goes. There is always an explanation for a good trade and a bad one... just look left until you find one. I know there are a select few here that are consistently profitable, but it is a difficult approach to master due to the amount of interpretative analyses involved. I know indicators are discounted here, but it does smooth out a lot of subjectivity and provides for more consistent (albeit later) decision making. I think every trader is different - skills, personality etc that may not ultimately favour pure PA decision making. For some, blending both may the best solution for them. I am finding myself falling into that camp to be honest. I will wait to see what you have to say. I will also copy this and post it in the classroom to see what others have to say. Below is a chart of what I think we are supposed to be doing. Its a chart of the EUR/USD. FIrst off lets start with the flags. I think the definition of a flag is when the top and bottom are liquidity gaps. In other words you find the area on the bottom that was broken with strong demand and the area on the top that was broken with strong demand. The area in the middle is your flag or CP. Right? My flags on here are marked with blue rectangles. The red lines are the extremes that we would look for price action and the middle is where we don't want to diddle! In other words there is either really clean ignored/broken SD above and below the CP or its just a flag. This is why the other areas that I marked with trend lines are not flags. These areas are just CP, thats why price moved through them. I don't know however why price stopped at the yellow line. That demand was spiked. If you look at the flag at the top with the red arrow, that is where I would look to short. Its an engulf from the area just to the left of it. For now it looks like price is compressing back up to the flag that did the engulfing. This means that I would look at the red lines of that flag on lower time frames for a sign. This could be a swap level, QM, engulf, or it might CP into the edge. QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU The Classroom #442 fxdaytrader Offline Trader Posts: 51 Thank you received: 72 Hi tradingjedi - this may not be the answer you are looking for, but may help you understand why price did what it did. In the context of the price action as visible on the 15M chart at that point in time (i.e. ignoring HTF levels etc), this is what I see: 1 and 2 are swing highs (i.e. price too expensive) 3 and 4 are swing lows (i.e. price too cheap) 5 price starts to turn, possibly in response to ignored supply to left - but who cares - because price does not move up and engulf anything 6 price pulls back to whatever tentative demand rests at 5 and then quickly shoots up and engulfs 1 and 2 - i.e. the Decision Point to engulf was in 6. Your initial entry (my blue box) was barely a RBR and not the origin of the decision to engulf - hence why it was ignored on the way back to fill the rest of the orders at 6. At the moment you can see the residual demand created by 5 and 6 being chewed up. I hope this helps a bit. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=425 23/35 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 18 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: Jambowlyai "OK - which one of you mother$%#kers wants to come second?" - CT Fletcher QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU The Classroom #443 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=425 24/35 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 18 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT tradingjedi Offline Trader Posts: 298 Thank you received: 123 fxdaytrader wrote: Hi tradingjedi - this may not be the answer you are looking for, but may help you understand why price did what it did. Hey Hornet... I think I understand what you may be going through.... Chart time typically increases ones knowledge from visually seeing price in action. Things tend to clutter the thought process by one or both of 2 issues I've seen over and over with trading supply & demand. First, the obvious, is when things don't go your way. You see a level, you trade it, and it's exactly wrong. Self doubt tends to wiggle its way in when it shouldn't. Not all trades work out how we planned, that's part of trading. The other issue, which often lends itself from the previous example, is we begin to overthink the concept. Is this a QM or not, does that look like compression, etc etc etc? Solution, step back. Perhaps start a journal, pinpoint when things go right and when they go wrong. IF is right, it is that simple. Part of the beauty of S&D trading is the ability of increasing the risk to reward ratio. Let the plan play itself out. You win some, you lose some, if you're reading the right levels and being patient for the market to come to you, in the end, you'll win a lot more than you lose. Hopefully this helps, if not, please share what some of the recent mistakes are. I'm sure members will try to provide insight. Good luck trader. My charts display the power of FTRs within the current move. Notice the FTRs as price went up got tested and usually produced a newer high, but also consumed the orders there. The ones that didn't produce newer highs after getting tested usually resulted in price moving through the just consumed FTR down to find the next lower untested FTR which then produced a new high. Then when price hit a HTF FTR on the supply side, price went all the way back to the last untested FTR. What I am working my way through atm is how does price handle opposing FTRs. I am guessing it just knocks price back to the current trends FTR. So what I am thinking is if price just tested that last untested ftr and reacted, then try to find the next opposing FTR and target that, but if there is a key s/r level between that ftr and current price, then price could form a new ftr before it hits the one you found, and then you would want to exit your position. Posts: 463 Thank you received: 910 Harsh, To my thinking we all get better when we try these things. I'm not any kind of eligible, and barely legible, but I'll have a crack at this. One of the defining elements of an FTR is a liquidity gap (wide bodied candle) away from the retrace. This would mean that your move B would invalidate A as an FTR. The move away from B would need to be a LQ to show an imbalance between supply and demand, and thus a higher probability of a reaction on the return. harshrthakkar wrote: To IF & Eligible Seniors ONLY - Please correct me if needed. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=550 20/34 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 23 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT There are 2 price points A & B..A has engulfed the Green circled area on the left while B hasnt engulfed.I want to know which price point makes a VALID FTR = DBR,A or B. This seems a good time to do it. There is a lot on here and it got kinda cramped, but hopefully its still legible. I just kept finding stuff and wanted to label it. There are still a few things I left off. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=550 30/34 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 23 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT In order to convey what I am thinking I used a new term. It should work till you or someone comes up with something better. STR - since price can't just keep going on forever, at some point it has to return back into the PAZ. But this is what really struck me while making this up: https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=550 31/34 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 23 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT 1) Price breaks a high and keeps going till supply hits it and leaves a HH 2) comes back to form an FTR at the old high 3) trades back up and makes a LH 4) falls back down to the FTR, it usually reacts for at least a small move to make another LH, but can fall through the FTR. Just know you may go into DD if your in the market and price fails to make a new high/low. 5) price then returns back into the PAZ that it left at 1. It may react to pockets of demand on the way down, but it ultimately wants the demand that created the HH. Now here is the kicker for me. If you draw a horizontal line from the high that was origanilly broke at 1, even though there are a bunch of candles now that you had to draw the line through, when price hits that demand and trades up and through the line it leaves an FTR at the line (the old high at 1). Once price fell back into the PAZ and reacted to demand, it tested the PAZ high again, even though there are a bunch of candles there this time, before continuing on the second time. I don't know how often this happens, and I need to do some more studies to make sure, but it happened 3 times on the one chart, all at HTF supply. Hope this makes as much sense to you guys as it does me. I have been studying a lot of the journals here and pulling it together as best I can. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=575 5/44 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 24 - RTM Community There are essentially 3 zones here, delineated by the zone in the middle. I have picked HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT up the FTR on the left at the top as being a place where a pause occurs at the edge of a PAZ. An engulf had already taken place and price had capped nicely, and the CP Index back up to the edge of the zone was a confluence indicator that price might be headed south when it eventually reaches the opposite end of this upper zone. Price moves between the opposite ends of the zones, and then decisions are made. The pause at the top demarks the a decision - price stalled, brielfy, and it could have gone north and returned into the zone and would have been an FO. But it doesnt. Its form manifests as price drops south and this becomes our FTR. Down in the middle, we have a flag limit and I also pick this up as an FTR. Price hhas halted here, and very well could have reversed back up. But it doesnt. It bases, and then its form again is made manifest, and it is decided it is still too expensive, in the middle of the value curve here. So this is another FTR. Down at the bottom I marked out what I see as being a key area of price action, and there is a nice FO DBR out and back in from underneath. This movement causes a nice RBR which engulfs the recent high. And in fact the box here could have started higher. After the engulf, one sign prices might be headed higher, the pullback comes back into the zone and bounces of a support level. This itself engulfs the last high that was formed (not shown), but the engulf had already happened, and readying to take a position had already ensued. Naturally, price makes its way to the opposite end of the zone (flag) and bounces back in from the FL. A few attempts are made, and indeed there are a few short trades here that I havent shown to avoid over cluttering the chart. The nice thing about all of this is that price comes back to where it wants to be - the origin. Within this area an engulf north happens (on the right at the bottom of the chart), and price bounces (naturally) back down from the FL. We have a double bottom and double top. Notice also just to the left, price makes a little CP as it rises, before price plummets. This is a nice movement for the pro money because it allows them to take the liquidity on the way down so that they can load up for the big move up to the top zone that they are look to. So price bounces from that small FL and makes its way back down to the demand zone that was created by the FTR all the way on the left. This double bottom is capped, and for sure this was a place to take an aggressive long position. From here price engulfs the latest high before retreating slightly (FTR). Well, when I first read this post I took it as if you thought it crazy that news would be used to fill pro money orders. I see now that it was more of a question just to that particular scenario. But I had already made a chart and the rest of this post, so I am posting in case it helps anyone else. Most everyone on this sight probably understands all this and could teach me even more, but it may be helpful to someone. I got it from the Larry Harris book Trading and Exchanges. Markets exist to find the value of the instrument being traded. In order to do this successfully it needs people who are informed of everything that effects that instrument to buy and sell it. These people are informed traders, pro money. People that are informed are not going to buy and sell against other informed traders. So if there were never any other participants, the market wouldn't function. Price would never move and https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=600 17/31 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 25 - RTM Community the value would never be found. In order to function, the market has to have uninformed HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT traders to take the other side of their orders. That is where the news comes in. The most informed traders position themselves in the market first, then their friends, then the people that pay monthly for news data, and then when the data the gets released at the news sites all over the internet the rest of the trading public and most uninformed come into the market and fill the pros profit taking orders. The markets have to function this way or they wouldn't function at all. I personally believe its all a bunch of B.S. I'll save you all from a diatribe though. I will say I it doesn't bother me one bit to profit from it, and help others who have unwittingly fell prey to their other ways of sucking up all the peoples wealth. Price moves between decision points until they no longer hold. Price comes down to the FL at 2, and dips below. We say that tells us price wants to go lower, but I think thats indirect, or rather too direct a statement. What really happens is the fresh demand that existed at the FL has now gone, and price dipped lower to the pocket of demand below before heading back up to supply. With that area now cleared, shorting at the top is a high probability/low risk trade because IF price does fall, the next place where demand is is at the origin of the up move - here is just above the P in point 2, where it says 2. Price then... I dont intend for this to be pedantic DT, sorry if it seems that way. I am just thinking about the mechanics of what is actually going on. I see that dipping down below the FL with 2, bouncing of the pocket of demand to the left - the SR flip. Once the demand there was gone, down it would go. Genius. Posts: 95 Thank you received: 219 aiden wrote: Hello, i Have a question on engulfing and fakeout for you experienced traders. hope you guys don't mind answering and shed some light on this. so i was reading faldot's journal (but it was also posted a lot by many), and some charts makes me think. Please correct me if i'm wrong on this: Both fakeout and Engulfing were taking out last low/high, correct? the question i have is, how do we know it was a fakeout and should not be treated as an engulfing or the other way around? or i take it completely wrong and in fact a fakeout is an engulfing? Thank you. cheers. For me there are four types or returns, 13/36 RT or FTB with normal respect to the zone. FO which engulfs and rejects the zone. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=700 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 29 - RTM Community ENG which engulfs and continues in the direction of the engulf. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT A fourth return is the fail to return. FO vs ENG When I see an engulf and wonder whether it is a FO or a ENG continuation I'll look for; the strength of the reaction after the FO/ENG 1 ... cp back to fresh zone (weak reaction), perfect to tighten your SL or if you're confident add another position. 2 ... lq engulfing fresh zone/dp/fl instantly (strong reaction), you should get out of your trade and wait for your entry signal 3 ... cplq (wedge... ) continuation after the FO, which should now be named ENG instead of FO. 4.... instead of reacting to the FO/ENG price could also simply form a DP/FL only to advance with strong LQ 5.... price can also cp back to the fresh levels only to consume them and hit you with LQ (hate it when that happens), but most of the time you will see a S level turn D before that happen, vice versa D turns S. So in general I look at the reaction + where the nearest zones are to counter this reaction (defensive range after effort) and I also base my conclusion on what the HTFs tell me, ofcourse. BTW good question, hopefully my little explaination helps :) cheers oz The following user(s) said Thank You: Mfinab, Tana, aiden, windorz, omidfxt, salivan QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU The Classroom #711 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=700 14/36 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 29 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT fatbugger Offline Trader Posts: 6 Thank you received: 8 Hi I think I understand what a quasimodo is , but what is a quasimodo level ? File Attachment: File Name: File Size: 0 KB https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=700 27/36 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 29 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Hello oneday, Not sure if I'm one with the best understanding of FTR's, but I'll give you my 2 pips regarding this. In a nutshell, FTR's = failed to return. Sounds simple enough? Failed to return to what? Well, I made it simple enough for myself to understand it. Failed to return to the range/flag/SR's AFTER an engulf, and it has to be the first attempt and, a short lived one. Well, you will see PLENTY PLENTY of FTR's in this case, coz it's the same case as engulfs, you'll see them all over the place. Your job, as a trader, is to pick the significant engulfs, hence the significant FTR's. In your chart, the FTR's that I considered good ones are D & G, and that's it. I used your chart to put some annotations. Hope it's not too cluttered. Hope it helps. A decision point in itself is powerfull. The word say it all "Decision" , meaning that someone decided if price was too cheap or too expansive at that particular moment in time. Once a decision has been made, you will always see some kind of follow through however you have to look at the whole picture in order to see where price is likely going to go. Let's say that price is at demand and a decision point was made to take price south. So what happened? Someone decide that price was too "expansive" and they want to see price going down but you should ask yourself where price is likely to go from there... Is there another fresh DP just bellow/above price? Is there enough room for price to move? Could it be that price went down so that they could buy back at a better price? To answer all this questions , you deffinately have to look at HTF's and see where price is and where it's trading to . More importantly it may signify that demand/supply is weakening. In this example, to me it shows the price action may be ready to turn to the next demand level. Looking left will help determine if there is supply available to facilitate the reversal. That spike up after the rounding could be viewed as compression to supply as well and by the looks of the reaction at supply, that is exactly what happened, real money clearing the way. And if you look carefully, you may be able to spot a quasi in there as well starting from the left tip where I indicated the "rounding PA". If you had the guts to short at that pinbar, great. If not, that small pullback after the drop is a retest into a flip zone another area to short. Remember this is how I see it and how I would view it as a potential set up and it reflects my style and trading plan which may not coincide with your goals. As i understand it you prefer to trade off H4. ...good option for reducing screen time. Your set ups should be very accurately traced from history on the remaining higher time frames.That would be D1, Weekly and Monthly. Make note of S/r and S/d static prices levels(horizontal lines). Draw them onto the higher tf...then go down to H4. Most platforms will automatically save what you have drawn. Visually check how your drawn levels relate to H4.and the current pa there.Trend lines are best drawn on the tf that you are trading off....to give a sense of gradient and an additional guide for your stop loss. Stops are subjective to pa but more importantly to your risk reward ratio. ( please see danandsuecos article on stop losses.)Typically you should only be risking 2-3% on a trade so if you cannot find a trade at that rr you should not take the trade imo.Subjective to pa you should be looking for a stop at next available s/r drawn from higher tf, ideally. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=50 23/37 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 3 - RTM Community I use same tf levels and/or nearest (to ratio) dp...indecision candles are a favourite of mine. HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT As mentioned above trend lines can give additional confirmation on setting your s/l, particularly when confluence of static levels occurr ( please read Markepedia on confluence) I hope this serves to help. Good luck with you trading. I had also noticed the base of that Spike you've marked, but I like to try to keep my live charts as clean as possible, otherwise I collect too much contradictory information and I don't need to be more confused than I usually am Spikes are interesting structures, and my view of them (rightly or wrongly) is that they are only reactions to Supply or Demand areas, not sources of it. That said, Supply or Demand areas can be created in their shadows - where exactly may not always be clear, so we might be best served waiting on what Price Action does in the shadow of the Spike and acting on that. Essentially that's what I did when I marked off the fresh Supply on that H1 chart in post #747. Unfortunately (or otherwise) I missed the short from that area because I was asleep! It would have yielded profit at TP1 (between 1 : 1 and 1.6 : 1 according to my way), but perhaps not much more (depending on what happens with Asian open tonight). The joke is, even though I used the conjunction of brand new H1 Supply as a supposed reaction to 'ancient' D1 Supply as the example for my question, the real reason for posting it is that I had actually favoured the long from that lower Demand area where price turned convincingly north (see one of my H1 charts below and also Spongy's Journal posts #75 and #76 for detail). If I had stuck with the original area instead of drilling into it to focus on a smaller area (that failed) I would have been well rewarded for my efforts and willingness to go long into a reaction from longer time-frame Supply, and certainly better off than shorting from either of those D1 or H1 Supply areas. It's because I see this time and again, where PA says one thing but history says another, that I thought clarification should be sought: I think it's a discussion which could benefit many others. I'm not saying that those areas should be ignored out of hand, but as they become older, perhaps less real attention should be paid to them when compared to what's happening right now. Maybe traders anticipate a turn because of that history, but we are better off awaiting the outcome of that anticipation instead of joining in with it. The fresh liquidity could be just what Pro Money needs to push prices further along if they aren't looking to book profits and turn. In my experience supply and demand zones have higher probability to work out when entries are made in the direction of engulfing waves. When trades are taken against trend, S/D zones are less likely to work out or give just a minor pull back often causing losses. Now if price engulfs down and reaches demand zone which is inside higher time frame demand zone lets say looking at H4 and price enters demand zone of Weekly chart then it becomes a different story. For example on H4 it might appear that price is waving down and engulfing down, but looking at weekly it might actually just retrace to demand zone of waves up and engulfs up. Higher time frames are stronger than lower ones so always need to keep them in mind where price is. The harder part is to enter a trade right, when waves are rising engulfing prior supply zones they rarely come/retrace back to new created demand zones and price runs away creating feelings of being right but not being in the market. What I would suggest to try is to go over and study all the information posted here, apply it to charts and see how it works, go over some of major journals see how they have applied that same information to their trading. And then just trade, trade and trade. After gaining experience your method will start to develop. I try to give my explanation, to me it seems to be a double Fakeout (just a beginner, I dont know if it makes sense) We are in a downtrend, point A engulfs previous Lower High, now we can think that price wants to reverse bullish and prepare to buy at demand area of previous Low or at QM level of the left shoulder, but price breaks the LL making a new Low (point B), so point A was only a fakeout. At this point we can imagine that the price wants to continue to go down because previous low is engulfed, preparing to sell at pullback (FTR), but price returns to the origin (no FTR) and breaks the previous High forming the new High C, so the point B was another Fakeout. Well, now...if price breaks the low of the point B, then C become another Fakeout, and if price breaks the High of C, then it is some kind of a messy bullish QM or H&S. I know it is confusing and maybe wrong, I hope you understand what I wanted to say, and sorry for bad english. Attachments: QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU The Classroom #800 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=775 27/29 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 32 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Andyfx Offline Trader Posts: 72 Thank you received: 107 I think that there is a bit of consufion about this term, because tipically people talk about Fakeout when price breaks a key level or a trendline and then come back inside the level, without specifying what happens next. As you wrote in your example, the High circled in red is a FO, because price broke high but then engulfed previous low. The low marked in your draw to me is only an engulf at this time. Now, if the price engulfs the previous high, then I consider that low an other Fakeout, if the price bounce below the previous High and then engulfs south, I consider the new LowerHigh a FTR or a pullback. The situation is your example looks like a Diamond pattern, but maybe we should be near S/D zone during a trend. I want to be able to "read the market" but I confess that I find the lingo confusing sometimes, especially when working through homework (which I will be posting to my own journal shortly.) In this post I'm going TRY to define some of the important words of the language of the market that are used at RTM. I tried to write this for someone with no market knowledge or experience in the hopes that I will learn by thinking through the concepts and taking little to nothing for granted. Disclaimer: these definitions are based on the current understanding of someone learning "marketese" and may be completely wrong! On some definitions I've included sources but feel free to chime in on any of these. Supply (S or SUP): sell orders that put pressure on price to fall. When Supply exceeds Demand, price falls. When Demand exceeds Supply, price rises. Demand (D or DEM): buy orders that put pressure on price to rise. When Demand exceeds Supply, price rises. When Supply exceeds Demand, price falls. Rally-Base-Drop (RBD): a 3-step process whereby: 1. demand exceeds supply and causes price to rise (Rally); 2. supply and demand find balance and price stabilizes https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=875 19/41 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 36 - RTM Community (Base); 3. supply exceeds demand and causes price to fall (Drop). The return to the HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT base is often tradable. Drop-Base-Rally (DBR): a 3-step process whereby: 1. supply exceeds demand and causes price to fall (Drop); 2. supply and demand find balance and price stabilizes (Base); 3. demand exceeds supply and causes price to rise (Rally). The return to the base is often tradable. Support-Resistance Flip (S/R Flip): a price point or zone that limits price's move downward, then breaks and later limits price's move upward. Resistance-Support Flip (R/S Flip): a price point or zone that limits price's move upward, then breaks and later limits price's move downward. Cap on Price (CAP): the base of a RBD or DBR. This is where price is limited from further upward movement in a rally or further downward movement in a drop. Source: Caps on Price article, If'd video on Caps, and even the article's name: "... RBD/DBR". Noticing the name alone was actually an aha moment for me last night. Pole: the sharp rally or drop that precedes a Flag. Flag: the base of a RBR or DBD. This is where price pauses to "catch its breath" before continuing on in the direction from which it came. Flags are also the "framework" for Flag Limits." Source: previous understand and the Flag Limit article and its name: "...DBD/RBR". This too was an aha moment for me last night. Flag Limit (FL): the edges of a Flag. Price often rallies from the bottom Flag Limit and drops from the top Flag Limit before eventually breaking outside of the Flag altogether. The Flag Limit that was Engulfed before price left the Flag is often tradable when price returns. Failure to Return (FTR): the same thing as a Flag Limit. Source: Ifmyante on FF speaking to Les_Paul - link: bit.ly/1pt3VRN I don't understand the "simple" part (yet), but since FTR's = FL's, should we drop using/trying to understand 1 of the 2? Or am I oversimplifying and misunderstanding If https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=875 20/41 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 36 - RTM Community and there really is a difference between FL's and FTR's? HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Engulf (ENG): two possible definitions: 1. the consumption of a Demand zone when price is coming from a Supply zone. The return to the Supply zone is sellable with the expectation that price will drop beyond the consumed zone that was Demand; 2. the consumption of a Supply zone when price is coming from a Demand zone. The return to the Demand zone is buyable with the expectation that price will rise beyond the consumed zone that was Supply. ** In either case, if there is no Engulf, then there is no Failure to Return. Source: Ifmayante on FF replying to Chica - link: bit.ly/1f9MJxg Compression (CP): indecision in the market where price ranges between Supply and Demand. With most (if not all) orders removed from the range, price can easily move through it the next time it arrives at the Compression. Price Action Zone (PAZ): the tradeable range between 2 Failure to Returns. Price moves between Failure to Returns until sufficient orders enter the market to Engulf a Failure to Return. At that point price moves between the Failure to Return that was just Engulfed and the next Failure to Return beyond it, which is another Price Action Zone. Thanks in advance for your time and thoughts! Actually, you are referring to Stacked Supply/Demand Zones. The screenshot below from this post , shows stacked Supply Zones. How do you find them? The same way that you find all supply and demand zones. Higher highs or lower lows will tell you the zones. We call HHs and LLs FTRs. Each FTR is a new level of supply or demand. You can see there are many ways to say the same thing. Even further, If is quoted as saying that an FTR is a Flag Limit ( here and here ). This screenshot from this article , shows the PAZs lined up in between the Supply and Demand Zones. The green zones are supply and demand zones that are stacked on top of one another. The PAZs are also stacked. It would appear that in order for stacked zones to exist there must be a trend. Posts: 52 Thank you received: 105 Hi Gigiocean, I have marked below an example of stacked supply zones. Here, by 'stacked zones' we mean that the Decision Points (Be it Supply or demand or FTRs) are arranged very closed to one another and so prices may ignore the intermediate levels to reach the next or outermost level (the highest supply zone here in example). And so there is no difference between both PAZs, it is just a matter of how they are 15/37 seen in the chart. QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU The Classroom #919 Kanzler Offline Associate Trader Posts: 196 Thank you received: 350 Just thought I would post something I'm watching so others can comment. The big picture is on the left panel. Price engulfs an important swing low from a recent series of lows at A and creates a flag limit 1. We zoom in on the middle panel to get a better picture of what's going on, and notice there may be an even better R/R opportunity. We see that when the low of our flag limit (C), which is itself a flag, was broken, we had an FTR or new flag limit created when price tried to get back into our zone at 2. Now that we have a place to watch for an entry, depending on how price moves back up to it, we need to consider a target. In the far right panel we see that we had an FTR which was holding up price. It has since been tapped a first time and now a second after price just recently dropped. To me this indicates the area is likely consumed. A good target might be a little above where I've marked the red horizontal rule at D, which is actually the FTR for a wider area if my analysis is correct. FTR/Flags are significant when they break an area of importance and continue in the direction of the break after forming. I second that. There are tons of zones, levels ENG, FO, FL, FTR etc on each chart on each timeframe Knowing them, spotting them, desribing them is easy for everyone. I think a child could do this after some training. But the thing which separates us from IF and other masters, is their abilities to spot those PAs which are important. And only few of them are indeed important. You can spot important ones when you deconstruct master's trades posted here on RTM. But you still will be miles away from them. Because knowing what's important is not enough still. And what's the most significant thing? It's knowing WHY are those pieces of PA important. Knowing WHAT price is going to do in case you are right, and what is it going to do in case you are wrong. What are you going to do in case you are right, and what are you going to do in case you are wrong is what makes great traders. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=925 27/32 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 38 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT After i started asking myself those questions each and every time i see a chart posted, or i take a trade myself, i was amazed how price behaves itself just the way i was expecting. And even if it's a small, tiny reaction, which doesn't even hit a half of a target, i still am statisfied. Because it's a step. Small one. But heading forward. I think a lot of ppl here can relate to these words "WHY" is always first, because there is nothing random in this world. Everything happens for a reason. The following user(s) said Thank You: polymorph, Lupy, windorz QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU The Classroom #948 polymorph Offline Trader Posts: 133 Thank you received: 231 Great words, Cleric! About 1.5 years ago I started to realize the difference between support/resistance trading and reading the market is found in the "why". "Why" isn't because there's a line I drew there or just because price bounced before - that doesn't take into account what is really going on, which is buying and selling and not just pretty shapes. Instead, "why" is because supply exceeded demand or demand exceeded supply, which leads to "who", as in whose supply and whose demand. Why did such and such happen? Because the IT's entered their orders and moved the price, and https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=925 28/32 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 38 - RTM Community thankfully they tip their hands (FO, ENG, etc.) and often show what is next. Regarding the Decision Point. Try to think about the definition of a decision point. I say when One side of Bull or Bears are winning and moving price further in their direction. We spot the DP where we see the last opposing power. Exp.: if Bulls win, we set the DP to where we see the last Seller. Usually that would be at the opening of the opposition bar. When either side wins a battle, it is called a Decision - a decision to move to the next level. What I think was confusing you, is that the next level did not set new high. it is not suppose to. But the decision was made to move higher. For the DP not creating new High, it was a hint sent to you, to tell you possible sellers are gaining strength. when last leg DP was broken, they were sending a louder message about their intentions for more selling. This is how I would look at it. Hope I am being more clear this time. Plus if we get some of the senior traders to chime in then we all benefit. When price breaks from a consolidation, range or cluster whether of short or long duration we have the makings of a potential DP. A clear break from a cluster with price moving clearly up or down with follow through is key. If there is no follow through then there really isn't a decision. If price stalls and moves back then IMO no decision was made. Price needs to engulf the previous price action and clearly break away. I chose this area in the chart below to illustrate something. Notice 1 and 2 are clear areas where price broke up with a bullish engulfing (BE). The first or lower BE broke out of a larger cluster than the one in BE 2. But price IMO did not truly make a decision to go much higher. Price stalled before getting to 3. If price had broken above 3 then that to me is a real decision because price would have engulfed the bearish price action to the left. In this case price did not engulf the bearish price action to the left so no real decision. Now this is in the context of the time frame shown. Having said all that above if you look at this on LTFs then in the context of LTFs these areas would probably be significant DPs. Also I want to stress again that DPs occur on all time frames. You may be able to clarify 23/32 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=75 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 4 - RTM Community the area on a LTF. Posts: 463 Thank you received: 910 Yep, you've got just about every FTR in there. The term "FTR" can be applied to pretty much every swing high in a downtrend (for example). If you can find the key FTRs, those where price has broken something significant prior to forming the FTR, those are the places to look to take trades from the "tip" of the FTR. I've chosen not to draw in every FTR on this chart, but only those where price has broken something significant (the black lines showing previous lows). At these line, price has the choice to go up, or keep dropping. This gives them their significance - they are previous decision points. In each case, price breaks them, and it's very last effort to go higher is the tip of the FTR. I just roughly marked these in yellow. Each of these area will have significant points of supply in them, and we look to trade down from these, based on price action in a lower time frame. I like the 3rd one down, it has broken 2 significant levels (the second, more minor level, is not marked in. It's about 1.0932) https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=1000 2/36 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 41 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: kkb, Slurpee1979, Bodostock, Kadox Roads? Well, and keep in mind I am still not a successful trader, I see it as the engulf in a signal that price will turn. In this USDCAD example, that entry I labeled #1 was the first time any supply had been engulfed on the way down after the 30M FL was engulfed. I see this happen a lot at market turns. I invite you to do the same. Pick a time frame and mark off the turns in the market (not spikes but turns). Often I see one of 3 things a) something local engulfed, retracement to source and then price leaves never to come back b) something local engulfed, retracement plus fake out and the price leaves and comes back for a QM c) something local engulfed, retracement, plus fake out, price leaves, comes back, QM fails and a diamond happens Whether it is a, b, or c depends on what is to the left usually. But I do see those scenarios happen all over the place. Try watching M1 turns for example. At the top of a move, a marker/flag usually appears. When that is engulfed south, that is usually the reverse signal. Time to look for an SR flip, locked in demand or some other structure to reverse on. An example from USDCAD today. Red lines are levels that get engulfed followed by returns to source. Again, this is just how I see it and I am still learning. I also wanted to add that this does not work everywhere on the chart. M1 levels get broken all the time. But an M1 level that forms in HTF supply, then gets engulfed south, well, that is something to pay attention to (in my opinion). https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=1025 3/31 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 42 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT GJ. If we think about a supply zone above the market and price faking out a previous high into that supply zone, we're inclined to think about it in terms of the supply zone relative to the previous high. So we're thinking "Why is the fakeout going to this supply zone above the high?", but if you turn it around and think "Why is this high below this supply zone?" it makes more sense. If when the price was rising initially, before the first high was made, the ITs sell early, before their final destination then they create that high, below our supply (fakeout) zone. So when price fakesout, really it's not reaching some extra supply zone, it's reaching the intended supply zone, but they've structured it in such a way as to deceive traders. Traders think the high is the final destination of price, but price is set up for a final (fake) move up to the supply zone above the high, to be quickly crushed and turned around. Paul Tudor Jones: "One thing I learned as a floor trader was that if, for example, the old high was at 56.80, there are probably going to be a lot of buy stops at 56.85. If the market is trading 70 aid, 75 offered, the whole trading ring has a vested interest in buying the market, touching off those stops, and liquidating into the stops--that is a very common ring practice. As an upstairs trader, I put that together with what Eli taught me. If I want to cover a position in that type of situation, I will liquidate half at 75, so that I won't have to worry about getting out of the entire position at the point where the stops are being hit. I will always liquidate half my position below new highs or lows and the remaining half beyond that point." BUT! I'm still really confused about engulfs! Help! I honestly think that there are a few loose pieces that needs to be tighten up. Perhaps it's to do with my profession - I am not a perfectionist but I like to be exact and precise about definition. So let's sort out any confusion regarding FTR vs FL once for all, agree? In case people still wonder what's FTR and what's FL. Let this diagram clear the confusion, and I am not inventing something new, I am just applying what I have learned from the articles in Marketpedia FTR = Failure to Return. I would actually prefer a more precise technical term. Because Failure to Return can be applied on any Fresh SD zones, i.e. after a zone is created, price has not returned to test it, so arguably any Fresh level = Failure to Return. The definition of FTR vs FL, according to the Marketpedia articles can be summarized in the following diagram: https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=1150 5/36 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 47 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT So essentially, an FL is created AFTER breaking a key barrier, and FL is drawn from Point 1 to Point 2. Where FTR is the MPL of the FL on this SAME TIMEFRAME. The next question I see many people have asked is, where do we look for trades? Is it at DP (decision to break), or at FL, or at FTR? MasterTrader Harry, basically put this to rest. according to him, - If after the creation of FL, price comes back to test the FL within a short period of time, then the FL has a high chance of turning price around. - However, if price does not come back, instead it leaves the area and go on a significant consolidation period, by the time it comes to this area, the FL is no longer a reliable trade location. So here is my takeaway from Harry's words: if price comes back after a long consolidation period away from the area, I would look at the FL as a FO level, and pay attention to the DP just beyond it as the area that has higher chance of turning price. I have also seen the word DP (Decision Point) causing confusion, because based on normal English definition, a DP is just Decision Point, and open up any charts, every point on the chart is a decision, every second there are decision to buy and sell by market participants. But in the spirit of RTM, my understanding is that DP is the 'kink' or 'pause' BEFORE the break of a key barrier. Whereas FL is the 'kink' AFTER the break of a barrier. So DP = Kink, FL = Kink, FTR = Kink but in a lower time scale than the parent FL. So a 'kink' is one of the most important revelation for me! When I see kinks, I see $$$$, https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=1150 6/36 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 47 - RTM Community All Hail the KINK! To explain a little bit deeper: a FTR, failure to return, isn't a specific part of the kink or the FL, it's the whole of the kink or FL. Say price moves up, but goes down briefly. There's some sort of barrier and therefore price doesn't retrace any deeper, ergo, fails to return, and goes back up. This whole move is, or rather: was, called the FTR. It's simply not the time yet for price to be turned but these kinks do represent some barriers. As Edge said, it is of critical essence to have a deep understanding of what the kink and/or FL does and why. @Trab Trading: I think you are correct in saying that you can also enter a trade a bit deeper into the FL. Doing so, you'll minimise the E to SL part of your trade, making it a higher R trade. I think I'm safe in saying that your SL would stay put at the same place, but your entry point moves closer to it, minimising your risk and maximising your reward. A FL remains a FL and doesn't need any refining when talking about entering a trade. You either do that at the edge of the FL, which is the safest point in terms of probability https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=1175 5/33 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 48 - RTM Community that your order is getting filled, or at the MPL of it. No need to get more specific than HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT that when explaining a trade, because those are the only two possible points of entry. I have taken new notes, and arrived at this new definition of FTR. So FTR is no longer the MPL of FL as presented in the article written by Les_Paul in Markepedia. Now, FTR is drawn exactly the same way as FL, referring to the diagram below. Point 1 = Furthest Advance AFTER breaking the Key Barrier to the left Point 2 = Deepest Retreat AFTER breaking the Key Barrier to the left Point 3 = Price has to move beyond point 1 in order to have an FTR The key difference between FTR and FL is: FL = FTR that has hit a TG! Now, I hear you probably screaming in exhaustion now - why can't you guys just stop talking about FTR!!!?!!! But there is a reason, because there is a 'gap' in the definition of FL. Warm regards, HRT Hi HRT, If you are new to Supply and Demand than I suggest to just try to trade the fresh zones. Just make sure that you know what the leading directions are from Higher Time Frames zones. Start your weekly analysis by looking at where price is on the HTF's. For example What 27/30 https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/classroom-and-trading-room/1517-the-classroom?start=100 7/27/2018 The Classroom - Page 5 - RTM Community is the direction price is trading at the moment on Monthly, Weekly, Daily, 4h. Are we HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT trading towards Supply or Demand? Did we just left Supply or Demand? Once you become comfortable at trading only fresh zones, you than can start looking at tested zones. I encourage you to get some screen time too. Draw your zones of intrest and watch how price reacts to it. This is a great way to learn more. Once you have your zones in place, look at the approach, is price compressing up towards your fresh supply/demand than it's a good thing. Let price show you what it wants to do and then trade in synch with it. Also, you really want to look at the potential target. If you have a fresh supply zone and there is not a lot of room for price to move, than as a beginner you can skip the opportunity and look for a beter place to trade elswhere. If you are new, I suggest you don't risk real money while learning. You can learn on a demo accout but yet treat it like it was real money. This is where you will get your discipline from. If you are really serious and dedicated about your future trading career, you got to be disciplined and put a lot of time and dedication to have this working. The good news for you is that you already found out that supply and demand is an important part of trading, this gives you an edge over other traders but like I said earlier there is a lot more to look at than just pure s/d but you'll discover all this set by step. So try to digest all the above and than make a decision. Are you willing to put the time and effort that is needed to become succesfull or are you not. Wishing you all the best anyway. I still find new things to learn here every day. Sometimes I feel overwhelmed by all this stuff. With all what you know now, if you'd recommend one or two strongest concepts, ideas or price situations (I try to avoid using ,,pattern", but cannot find a better word) to a noob to acquire first, what would it be?
